summary: Jesus compares the kingdom of God to seed scattered on the ground: it sprouts and grows while the farmer sleeps, until the ripe grain is ready for the sickle.
key_insight: The farmer does only two things: he scatters the seed and, at the end, puts in the sickle. Everything between happens without him: “he himself does not know how,” and the earth yields crops “by itself.”
story: Jesus was still teaching by the Sea of Galilee. After the parable of the sower and His warning to take heed what they heard, He gave them another picture.

“The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground.” Then the man goes about his days. He sleeps by night and rises by day, and all the while the seed sprouts and grows, “he himself does not know how.”
“For the earth yields crops by itself: first the blade, then the head, after that the full grain in the head.”

“But when the grain ripens, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” Mark records no explanation of this parable. Jesus went straight on to another picture of the kingdom, the mustard seed.

scene.label: “By itself”
scene.text: Mark’s Greek word is automatē, the root of the English word automatic. It appears only once more in the New Testament, when the iron gate of the prison opened for Peter and the angel “of its own accord” (Acts 12:10). In both places no human hand is at work.

scene.label: The growing season
scene.text: In Galilee grain was sown in late autumn, after the first rains softened the ground, and harvested in spring, barley first and wheat a few weeks later. For months a farmer could do little but wait while the green shoots came up, then the heads, then the filling grain.

scene.label: Night and day
scene.text: Mark’s order, “sleep by night and rise by day,” puts night first, perhaps reflecting the Jewish way of counting a day from sunset (Genesis 1:5). The phrase pictures ordinary days passing one after another while the farmer simply lives.

scene.label: The sickle
scene.text: Grain was cut by hand with a short, curved sickle. Jesus’ words echo Joel’s picture of God’s final judgment: “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe” (Joel 3:13). Revelation uses the same picture for the end of the age (Revelation 14:15).

witnesses.mark: This is the one parable only Mark records. At the same point in his chapter of parables, between the sower and the mustard seed, Matthew tells of the wheat and the tares; Mark gives this quiet picture of seed growing unseen, right after Jesus’ promise that nothing hidden will stay hidden (4:22). Even here Mark’s favorite word appears: “immediately” the farmer puts in the sickle.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is entirely calm about the kingdom’s progress. Its growth does not depend on human strength or understanding, and He speaks of its end as certain: “the harvest has come.”
seeing.living: The farmer sowed and went to bed; he did not dig up the seed each morning to see whether it was working. Those who teach children, speak of Christ to a friend or preach week after week can do the same: sow faithfully, sleep, and leave the growing to God. The harvest is His to bring, and it will come at the right time.
seeing.ponder: What seed have you sown that you keep digging up to check on, and can you trust God with the part only He can do?

preaching.big_idea: We scatter the seed and sleep; God grows His kingdom, and the harvest will surely come.
preaching.watch_for: The growth comes in stages, “first the blade, then the head, after that the full grain in the head” (v. 28), and the farmer waits through each one. Some take the sower to be Jesus, others any servant who sows the word, but the weight of the parable falls on the seed and the soil, not on the man.
